newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament may change controversial law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament may change controversial law.

text.p: Slovakia's ruling coalition may modify a law drawing heavily on communist-era anti-subversion legislation which has been heavily criticised by the West, a senior coalition member said on Thursday.

Jan Cuper, a leading member of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), said the controversial "protection of the republic" legislation could be withdrawn from the current session of parliament.

The United States and the European Union have criticised the law, an amendment to the criminal code, and other legislation by the Meciar government. Washington says it is worried that Slovakia's commitment to democracy is slipping.

Under the amendment people could be punished for acts such as organising anti-government demonstrations. Some of its wording is almost identical to anti-subversion laws scrapped after the 1989 fall of communism.
President Michal Kovac refused to sign the amendment earlier this year but a simple parliamentary majority can overturn a presidential veto.
"I think the criminal code will be withdrawn from the agenda," Cuper told Reuters. "We persuaded our coalition partners that it was necessary to alter it, to make it compatible (with EU standards)."

He denied there was a direct relationship between the likely withdrawal of the penal code amendment and expressions of grave concern from the United States and EU about democratic reforms and the rule of law in Slovakia.

Cuper said the HZDS was working on a new version of the law, which was originally drafted by a junior coalition partner, the ultra-right nationalist Slovak National Party (SNS), as a price for supporting a treaty with neighbouring Hungary.
On Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador Ralph Johnson repeated Washington's concerns over a number of Slovak laws "which do not conform to generally accepted notions of a democratic society".
EU ambassador Georgios Zavvos said on the same day there was much work ahead if Slovakia was to earn a place in Western structures.

On Wednesday Eric Newsom, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State, told Slovakia it must demonstrate its active commitment to democracy to gain acceptance in an expanded NATO and other Western structures.

On Wednesday the coalition appeared to ignore the warnings by passing two other laws criticised by the West and rejected by Kovac -- a law on public prosecution and a law extending government control over universities.

Parliament's attitude was echoed by Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik who was quoted by the media as saying: "I see no reason for the ministry to react to statements of ambassadors. There are plenty of them here."
